persona.bio: Office coordinator for an office of about 70 people. In her own words: I am an office coordinator for an office of about 70 people. I prepare and organize lunch for everyone. I order drinks, restock the fridges and keep the office clean and organized. I take care of the plants and general maintenance. I handle special orders and preparations for company events. I coordinate suppliers and make sure we have what we need. I am the person everyone comes to when something is missing or needs fixing. If the printer runs out of ink I find a replacement, and if we have none I order more. She works in Outlook, Teams and Excel, on a computer and on her phone. She is new to AI and has never really used it. She is an employee and is not sure what her company allows.

steps.firstStep: I’m an office coordinator for an office of about 70 people. I regularly email suppliers to order lunch and restock drinks. Write a short, polite email to a supplier. Keep it under 90 words, friendly and clear. Include the date, the number of people, any dietary needs and the items to restock. End the email by asking for their availability and delivery time. Here are this time’s details: [paste the order details here].

steps.note: I am an office coordinator for an office of about 70 people. I handle lunch, drinks, fridge restocking, supplies, company events and suppliers, and I am the person people come to when something is missing or broken. I write to coworkers, suppliers and my manager. Keep the tone friendly, clear and direct, and keep messages short unless I ask for more. Use plain words. Never add details I did not give you, like prices, quantities, dates or policies. If something is missing, put it in square brackets so I can fill it in. Always give me a draft I can read and change before it goes out.

steps.title: Your supplier emails, written with AI
steps.read: Supplier emails get written in Claude each time they come up. You paste one message with today’s details, and Claude drafts the email for you to read and send. That way every email starts from your situation and your tone instead of a blank page.

material.label: Message for supplier emails
items: I am an office coordinator for an office of about 70 people. Please write an email to a supplier in my voice, friendly, clear and short. The email is about [what I need, like a lunch order, drinks, restocking or printer ink]. Details for today: [items and quantities], needed by [day and time], delivery to [address or location], dietary needs [for example 2 vegetarian and 1 gluten free]. Do not add prices, policies or details I did not give you. If something is missing, put it in square brackets. Give me a subject line and the email, ready for me to read and change before I send it.

steps.title: Your event plans, with a saved assistant
steps.read: Your event plans live in a saved Claude assistant that already knows your office, your tone and your usual suppliers. You hand it the event and it drafts the details in your voice, and you read and change them before anything goes out. That way you stop rewriting the same plan from scratch for every event.

material.label: Instructions for your assistant
items: You help me plan company events. I am an office coordinator for an office of about 70 people. I handle lunch, drinks, supplies, suppliers and anything that needs fixing, so I plan events from start to finish. When I describe an event, write the plan or the message I ask for in my voice: friendly, clear and plain, with short sentences. Cover the date, the headcount, food and drinks, dietary needs, setup, suppliers to contact and what needs to be ready beforehand. Never invent prices, quantities, dates, vendors or company rules. When a detail is missing, put it in square brackets so I can fill it in. Do not give legal, safety or financial advice. Give me a draft I can read and change, with a short checklist of what I still need to confirm.

material.label: Examples to start with
items: Event: team lunch on [day] for [number] people. Plan: Order lunch from [caterer] by [day]. Include [number] vegetarian and [number] gluten free options. Ask for delivery at [time]. Set up drinks, plates and napkins in [room]. Send the team a note on [day] asking for dietary needs.

Event: end of quarter celebration on [date]. Plan: Confirm the headcount with my manager. Ask [supplier] for a quote for food and drinks. Book [room] and set up chairs and tables the day before. Remind everyone [number] days ahead with the time and place.

Event: visitor day at the office on [date]. Plan: Email [supplier] to order coffee, water and snacks for [number] guests. Tidy the common areas and restock the fridges the day before. Tell the team where guests will park and where to meet them.

safeUse: Never type coworker names, health or allergy details tied to a person, home addresses or phone numbers into Claude. Use square brackets or roles instead.
Never paste account numbers, payment card details, login details or supplier contract terms.
Keep dietary needs as counts, like 2 vegetarian, and not names.
Read every email and plan before it goes out, and check quantities, dates and prices yourself.
Check with your manager or IT before you use Claude for work, and ask about linking your work email.
steps.askMessage: Hi [manager or IT name], I would like to know which AI tools the company has approved and what I may use them for. I am thinking of using one to draft supplier emails and to plan company events, like lunches and drinks orders. I would not put coworker names, personal details or payment information into it, and I would read everything before it is sent. Could you let me know what is allowed, and whether linking my work email to an AI tool needs approval first?

design.today: You write supplier emails often, and each one takes a fresh start. Your work happens in Outlook, text messages and on paper.
design.newWay: You keep one saved assistant that knows your usual suppliers, your tone and the details a supplier needs, like item, amount and delivery day. You type or paste the few facts for each order, such as oat milk and sparkling water for the fridges, and it hands back a finished draft. You copy it into Outlook yourself, so the AI never touches your work email. Each email stops being a fresh start, and nothing about your company's rules is put at risk while you wait to hear whether AI is allowed.

fixes: The count is off: check that every choice is spelled exactly as in the drop down list.
A dietary need is missing from the email: copy the highlighted rows into the dietary line.
The email sounds too long: ask Claude to shorten it and keep all the counts.
